verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on three independent grounds.

(1) Nothing is missing. The kind label 'missing-heading' is factually wrong. I rendered page 282 at 300 dpi (E:/Temp/specrecon/v282/spec_p282.png) and read it against E:/Temp/specrecon/v282/page-282.md and the master specs/ISO_COBOL.md (lines 12271-12318). Every heading printed on the page -- 9.3.13 Parameterized interfaces, 9.3.14 Object life cycle, 9.3.14.1 General, 9.3.14.2 Life cycle for factory objects, 9.3.14.3 Life cycle for instance objects, 9.4 User-defined functions -- is present in the markdown with its number and title character-for-character identical. Every body paragraph and the NOTE under 9.3.14.3 are present. Not one word of PDF content is absent, reordered, or altered. The only text beyond the printed page is the tail of the 9.4 opening paragraph, which continues onto page 283 -- ordinary page-break furniture.

(2) The PDF asserts no heading level, so the markdown cannot contradict it. I extracted the PDF span metadata directly (PyMuPDF, pdf page index 281). EVERY bold heading on page 282 is the same font at the same size at the same left margin: Cambria,Bold 11.67 pt at x=63.5 -- 9.3.13 (y=90.2), 9.3.14 (y=330.5), 9.3.14.1 (y=355.8), 9.3.14.2 (y=406.3), 9.3.14.3 (y=482.2) and 9.4 (y=643.7). Page 281's 9.3.10/9.3.11/9.3.12 are likewise Cambria,Bold 11.67 pt. A second-level subclause (9.4), a third-level subsection (9.3.13) and a fourth-level subsection (9.3.14.1) are typographically INDISTINGUISHABLE in the source document. The claim's own premise -- 'printed identically to 9.3.12' -- is true but self-defeating: 9.4 is printed identically to 9.3.12 as well. In this spec the hierarchy is carried solely by the dotted numbering, and the markdown preserves that numbering verbatim, plus anchors that encode the correct depth (section-9-3-13, section-9-3-14-1, section-9-4). No information present in the PDF has been lost. The difference is markdown formatting with no PDF counterpart -- it does not change meaning.

(3) The claim misdescribes the markdown it cites. It argues '9.4 at level 2 while its sibling ### 9.1 Files is level 3', implying 9.4 is the deviant. The actual file shows the opposite: line 11007 '## 9 I-O, objects, and user-defined functions', 11010 '### 9.1 Files', 11692 '## 9.2 Screens', 11829 '## 9.3 Objects', 12314 '## 9.4 User-defined functions'. 9.4 matches two of its three siblings and matches the parent clause; 9.1 is the lone outlier. The claim picked the one counter-example and inverted the direction of the anomaly.

Finally, the heading-depth noise is document-wide transcription jitter, not a page-282 event: within clause 9.1 alone the file has '#### 9.1.1' adjacent to '## 9.1.3', '### 9.1.7.2' adjacent to '## 9.1.7.3', and '### 9.1.13.7' adjacent to '## 9.1.13.8'. Filing it as a per-page PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy is a category error; if the owner wants uniform outline depth that is a single global normalization pass over the transcription, driven by the section numbers, not a reconciliation finding against page 282.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. All six headings and all body text on page 282 are transcribed completely and correctly; the PDF renders 9.3.13, 9.3.14, 9.3.14.1-.3 and 9.4 in one identical style (Cambria,Bold 11.67 pt, x=63.5), so it encodes no heading level for the markdown to contradict -- the hierarchy lives in the dotted numbering, which is preserved exactly. The markdown's inconsistent '#' depth is document-wide transcription jitter (e.g. '#### 9.1.1' beside '## 9.1.3'), addressable by one global renumber-from-section-number normalization, not a page-282 reconciliation item. The claim is additionally inaccurate: it is labelled 'missing-heading' though nothing is missing, and its 9.4-vs-9.1 evidence is inverted -- '## 9.2 Screens', '## 9.3 Objects' and the parent '## 9 I-O, objects, and user-defined functions' are all level 2, making '### 9.1 Files' the outlier rather than 9.4.
